title: Packet Capture
summary: Packet capture is the recording of network traffic at the frame level for later analysis, produced either by copying traffic to a monitoring interface, by a hardware tap inserted in the link, or by a capture agent on a host that sees only its own traffic. Each captured frame is normally written with a timestamp, and the analysis software decodes protocol layers so an analyst can follow a conversation, measure timing and reconstruct what was transferred. It underpins incident response, where the capture may be the only record of an intrusion that left little on disk, and it is equally central to performance troubleshooting, control validation and signature development. The practical problems are volume, position and law: full packet capture of a busy link generates enormous data that must be filtered, rotated and stored, encryption such as TLS prevents reading payloads unless keys or endpoints are available, and a capture taken at the wrong point in an asymmetric path sees only half the conversation. It also collects personal data and credentials in transit, so retention, access control and legal basis are part of the engineering, not an afterthought. The common mistake is to treat capture as a magic answer without planning storage, placement and privacy, and then discovering after an incident that the needed window was overwritten or never traversed the sensor at all.

beginner.definition: A packet is a small piece of data travelling across a network. Packet capture means making a copy of those pieces as they pass, so you can study them later. The copy is saved with the exact time each piece arrived. Analysts use it to understand what happened on a network. It is like a recording of a phone call, but for computers.
beginner.whyItMatters: When something goes wrong, memory of the event is often gone, but the recording remains. It shows which computer talked to which, and when, which helps you find the cause. It also proves what actually happened, instead of relying on someone's memory. Without it, an investigation may end with guesses. The catch is that recordings grow very large. They may also contain private information, so plan where to keep them and for how long.
howItWorks: You choose a point on the network where the traffic you care about passes through.
A copy of that traffic is sent to a tool, while the original traffic continues normally.
The tool saves each piece with a timestamp and details such as addresses and ports.
Software then groups the pieces into conversations and decodes the protocol.
If the traffic is encrypted, you can still see who talked to whom and how much.
You store the files with limits on size and age, and restrict who may read them.
beginner.example: Picture a post office that photographs every parcel passing its counter. Each photo records the sender, the destination and the exact time. If a parcel is reported missing, staff can replay the photos and see what happened. Photographing every parcel produces a huge archive and shows personal details. So the office keeps photos briefly and lets only supervisors view them.
takeaways: Location matters: a capture only shows traffic that actually passes the sensor.
Encryption hides content but still reveals who communicated with whom and when.
Plan storage, retention and privacy rules before you switch capture on.

objectives: Define packet capture and explain the difference between a tap, a span port and host based capture.
Describe what metadata remains visible in an encrypted capture and what becomes unreadable.
Explain how capture placement affects whether both directions of a conversation are recorded.
Identify investigation and troubleshooting tasks where packet capture provides decisive evidence.
Outline retention, access control and privacy considerations for stored capture data.
